title: AgentOrch: How Close Can Global Orchestration Come to Step-by-Step Interaction?
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:AgentOrch: How Close Can Global Orchestration Come to Step-by-Step Interaction?
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Enterprise workflow agents typically rely on step-by-step interaction (Step-by-Step): the agent executes an action, observes its result, and invokes a large language model (LLM) again to decide the next step. Global orchestration (Global) instead generates a complete executable workflow in advance and executes it without further LLM calls, substantially reducing inference overhead, but it remains less accurate than Step-by-Step. We study how close Global can come to Step-by-Step and what narrows the remaining gap. We introduce AgentOrch, a benchmark that directly compares global orchestration with step-by-step interaction on 650 enterprise SOPs and 3,220 runtime variants under matched tools, environments, and evaluation. Step-by-Step remains more accurate for every evaluated model, but the gap has shrunk by about 79% from early models to the strongest recent model. We identify three routes to further narrowing this gap. Incremental workflow construction improves Global accuracy by an average of 9.98 percentage points (pp) without runtime execution feedback. Revising complete workflows with execution feedback improves all evaluated models, including 6.13 pp on held-out runtime variants. Targeted training on complete workflows improves accuracy by an average of 12.18 pp across all five trained models. Although a gap remains, global orchestration offers a promising path toward enterprise agents that deliver higher accuracy with fewer LLM calls.

report.summary: AgentOrch benchmark finds global workflow orchestration still trails step-by-step agents but has narrowed the accuracy gap by 79%, with targeted training and feedback further closing it.
report.background: Enterprise agents automate standard operating procedures (SOPs) by calling tools and LLMs. The common step-by-step pattern executes one action, observes the result, then asks an LLM to choose the next step. It is accurate but expensive and slow because every step needs inference. Global orchestration instead generates a complete executable workflow upfront and runs it without further LLM calls, cutting overhead but risking brittle execution when runtime conditions vary. AgentOrch provides a matched comparison across 650 enterprise SOPs and 3,220 runtime variants, using the same tools, environments, and evaluation. It measures how close global orchestration can get to step-by-step interaction and tests interventions that narrow the remaining accuracy gap.
key_points: AgentOrch directly compares two enterprise-agent strategies under matched conditions: step-by-step interaction, which calls an LLM after every action, and global orchestration, which compiles a full workflow before execution. The benchmark uses 650 enterprise SOPs and 3,220 runtime variants, making the accuracy and efficiency trade-off measurable rather than anecdotal.

Step-by-step interaction remains more accurate for every model tested, but the gap is shrinking. From early models to the strongest recent model, the accuracy difference fell by about 79%, suggesting that stronger LLMs are getting better at planning complete workflows without per-step reasoning.

The paper identifies three ways to improve global orchestration. Incremental workflow construction adds an average 9.98 percentage points without runtime feedback. Revising complete workflows using execution feedback improves all tested models, including 6.13 points on held-out runtime variants. Targeted training on complete workflows adds 12.18 points across five trained models.

Global orchestration’s main advantage is fewer LLM calls, which can reduce inference cost and latency in enterprise automation. The remaining accuracy gap means it is not yet a universal replacement for step-by-step agents, especially in high-stakes or highly variable SOPs where runtime feedback and verification matter.
report.impact: The results push enterprise-agent design toward a compile-then-execute model rather than pure per-step reasoning. For the AI industry, AgentOrch provides a matched benchmark that separates planning quality from tool access and environment differences, making claims about orchestration more comparable. Developers can treat global orchestration as a cost-saving option, but should pair it with incremental construction, execution-feedback revision, or targeted training on complete workflows. The biggest practical lesson is hybrid design: generate a workflow upfront, then use feedback loops where runtime variance is high. For regular users, the payoff could be faster, cheaper agents for routine SOPs, while high-stakes tasks may still need step-by-step checks or human verification until the accuracy gap closes further.
report.tools: Watch for the AgentOrch benchmark release and its evaluation harness. To follow up, compare it with open-source agent orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, workflow engines such as Temporal or Airflow, and LLM workflow-planning libraries. These let developers test global versus incremental workflow generation, add execution-feedback revision, and measure accuracy against inference-call savings in enterprise SOP automation.
